Pangenomic evolutionary possibilities for Darwin’s abominable mystery
abstract: Telomere-to-telomere pangenomes reveal a previously undersampled layer of genome evolution that may help explain rapid plant diversification vis-à-vis Darwin's abominable mystery.

title: Stomatal biology meets multimodal foundation model-driven AI
abstract: Stomata regulate plant growth and environmental responses through their control of gas exchange and transpiration. However, high-throughput stomatal phenotyping and the integration of phenotypic, genetic, and multiomics data remain major challenges for biological discovery and for understanding stomatal function in plants. Here, we review emerging imaging technologies and foundation models for stomatal biology and discuss how advances in AI could transform plant stomatal research. The rapid accumulation of large-scale phenotypic, genetic, and omics datasets requires systematic integration of heterogeneous data and their interpretation to uncover mechanisms of stomatal regulation within a unified reasoning framework. Therefore, we propose a stomatal phenotyping and analysis agent framework that connects these pipelines to accelerate hypothesis generation, phenotype-genotype analysis, discovery of biological function, and crop improvement.

title: Trade-offs determine plant responses to ozone pollution
abstract: Tropospheric ozone (O 3) triggers interconnected plant responses across physiological, whole-plant, and ecological scales. This review presents trade-offs as a unifying framework for understanding these responses. Stomatal closure limits both O 3 entry and carbon gain, creating an avoidance-photosynthesis trade-off and influencing water relations. Resulting carbon constraints drive allocation trade-offs between growth and defense and between roots and shoots. These shifts cascade to trophic interactions, altering plant-insect and plant-microbe dynamics. In agriculture, differential sensitivity of grain biomass and nutrient accumulation produces an apparent yield-quality trade-off. This framework explains how O 3 interacts with other global changes, with outcomes varying by stress intensity and plant type. Deciphering this hierarchy of interconnected trade-offs is crucial for predicting future impacts and guiding crop breeding and conservation.

title: Oxygen and redox regulation of plant thermomorphogenesis
abstract: Plant thermomorphogenesis represents the adjustment of growth to warm ambient temperatures. The mechanism has long been organised around the transcription factor PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4) and the thermosensors that act upon it. Internal circadian control and external light intensity and quality have been the primary contexts that gate thermosensor-PIF signal transduction. Here, we argue that cellular oxygen and the reduction/oxidation (redox) state of the cell form additional layers that gate or calibrate thermosensing signal transduction. Current evidence points to discrete mechanisms across spatial or developmental contexts, through which oxygen availability or redox-dependent protein modifications control thermomorphogenic signalling, largely downstream of or independent of PIF4. Logical argument suggests that significant mechanisms and crosstalk between oxygen and redox signalling and thermosensing remain to be revealed.

title: Tracking newly synthesised proteins in plants
abstract: Protein synthesis rate is distinct from steady-state protein abundance and must be measured independently to understand how cells regulate protein levels and respond to environments. Technologies used to predict or directly quantify protein synthesis include ribosome profiling, radioactive and stable isotope labelling, and bioorthogonal noncanonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT). Here, we emphasise BONCAT's potential in plants, which, when combined with click-chemistry, enables the detection, enrichment, and characterisation of newly synthesised proteins themselves. We summarise lessons from BONCAT applications in cell-free systems, microbes, mammalian cells, and animals and evaluate its potential in plants. Establishing robust BONCAT approaches in plants can advance studies in proteome regulation, stress responses, development, circadian biology, and plant-microbe interactions.

title: The redox–phytohormone nexus, illustrated by the jasmonate paradigm
abstract: Redox-sensitive protein switches and transcriptional networks are integral to phytohormone signaling networks. The jasmonate (JA) signaling pathway, which incorporates the coronatine insensitive 1 (COI1)-Jasmonate ZIM-domain (JAZ) co-receptor and the MYC2 transcription factor, is a relatively recent evolutionary innovation that has emerged only in land plants. Earlier JA signaling systems relied on electrophilic oxylipins, such as 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid (OPDA) and dinor-12-oxo-10,15(Z)-phytodienoic acid (dn-OPDA), and reactive oxygen species (ROS), particularly H 2 O 2 . All plant 14-3-3 proteins, such as General regulatory factor 8 (GRF8), contain a conserved redox-sensitive cysteine. Sulfenylation of GRF8 relieves inhibition of MYC2, thereby facilitating JA signaling in arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana). This mechanism may represent a primordial oxylipin signaling system, overlain by the more recent COI1-JAZ system, revealing hormone signaling plasticity that can be targeted for engineering stress-resilient crops.

title: From genes to farms: a modern breeding revolution
abstract: Feeding a growing world demands smarter crop breeding. A recent study by Yao et al. analysed 108 maize hybrids across three breeding eras, identifying favourable alleles for plant architecture and dense planting. Pyramiding these alleles into elite parental lines while retaining yield-related alleles produced improved hybrids, demonstrating measurable yield gains.

title: The heat is on for plant nitrogen nutrition
abstract: Global warming leads to increased average atmospheric temperatures, which will inevitably have an impact on plant growth and crop yields. It is essential to understand how plant nutrition will be affected by elevated temperatures. Nitrogen is one of the major mineral nutrients, and its uptake is enhanced during the light period, peaking at the day/night transition, whereas its storage, especially in the form of nitrate (NO 3 - ), is favoured in the dark. Given the overlap between light and temperature responses, we review the interaction between nitrogen nutrition and light responses and place this in the context of new findings on temperature sensing. We also suggest new hypotheses on the potential links between temperature and NO 3 - homeostasis.

title: Creating the first synthetic plastid genome in plants
abstract: Over the last decade, there has been a shift in biotechnology from genome reading (sequencing) to genome writing (engineering). While significant progress has been made in prokaryotes and yeast, genome writing remains in its infancy in plants. Unlike their complex nuclear genomes, the compact and biotechnologically attractive plastid genome represents an ideal target to launch plant genome writing at scale.

title: Reconsidering photorespiration through the eyes of guard cells
abstract: Sustainable agriculture, climate change, and a growing global population require resilient crops that deliver more with fewer resources. Leaf gas exchange is an important physiological crossroads, where CO 2 uptake and water loss must be balanced, especially under hotter, drier, and more variable extreme environmental conditions. We argue that an overlooked leverage point lies at the interface between photorespiration and stomatal regulation. Although each process is well described in isolation, how photorespiration can shape guard cell opening remains unresolved. We describe the impact of photorespiration on stomatal opening, discuss whether this involves photorespiration in mesophyll cells, guard cells, or both cell types, propose potential underlying mechanisms, and highlight photorespiration-stomata interactions as a target to improve plant water-use efficiency and resilience without compromising yield.

title: Life on the chalk: mechanisms of plant sensing and adaptation to high-pH soils
abstract: Soil pH is a fundamental determinant of plant health, governing nutrient availability and physiological processes in the rhizosphere. High pH, especially in calcareous soils, reduces the solubility of iron, phosphorus, zinc, and manganese, causing nutrient deficiency, chlorosis, and yield loss. In this review, we summarize recent advances in plant responses to high-pH stress. Plants sense high external pH through changes in membrane potential and the rapid alkalinization factor-FERONIA and plant peptide containing sulfated tyrosine 1-PSY1R systems that regulate plasma membrane H + -ATPase activity. Hormonal signaling, particularly via auxin, integrates pH sensing with root growth regulation and ion homeostasis. Key regulators such as PHOSPHATE STARVATION RESPONSE 1, IRON MAN peptides, and basic leucine zipper 19/23 coordinate nutrient homeostasis under high-pH stress. We further discuss calcicole adaptations, microbial partnerships, and soil management practices that mitigate high-pH stress.

title: extracellular ATP: an emerging primer for plant stress memory
abstract: Plants can retain information from prior stress exposure as strong and durable memory, but the proximal signals that establish the primed state remain elusive. Extracellular ATP (eATP), a ubiquitous damage-associated molecular pattern released upon cellular perturbation, is emerging as an early orchestrator of plant stress adaptation. Herein, we advance a framework positioning eATP as a regulatory hub that integrates stress perception via the purinoceptor 2K1/2 (P2K1/2), amplifies Ca 2+ and reactive oxygen species signaling, and interfaces with phytohormone networks, energy sensors, chromatin regulation, and noncoding RNAs. We propose eATP as an integrative priming hub, explicitly separating established signaling from hypothesized epigenetic memory, and discuss how this framework can guide plant resilience strategies.

title: Evolutionary flexibility in final steps of salicylic acid biosynthesis
abstract: The discovery of benzyl alcohol biosynthetic enzymes, by Lee et al. and Zhang et al., resolves a decades-old gap in the 'post-phenylalanine ammonia-lyase' (post-PAL) salicylic acid (SA) pathway. Pathway completion reveals metabolic flexibility and substantial evolutionary plasticity, with distinct enzyme modules and subcellular organization generating the same intermediate across plant lineages. Thus, conserved metabolic function can coexist with divergent biochemical architecture.

title: Cross-kingdom volatile networks shape plant resilience
abstract: Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are interpreted as transient, unidirectional signals in plant-microbe interactions. We argue that this reductionist framing obscures their emergent role as regulators of ecological network dynamics, influencing stability-associated properties of plant-microbe systems. We propose a conceptual framework based on five principles (gradient logic, blend emergence, feedback reciprocity, threshold switching, and multiscale coupling) and use it to generate falsifiable predictions for how plant-derived and microbial VOCs operate as a cross-kingdom regulatory network shaping microbiome assembly, plant physiological plasticity, and multitrophic interactions. Key mechanistic gaps are critically evaluated alongside testable approaches for probing volatile-mediated ecological dynamics. Viewing volatile networks as adaptive ecological infrastructure reframes plant-microbiome resilience with implications for sustainable agriculture and ecological restoration under global change.
